2.2 — Spikes: Physics, Damage & Death

You built a coin you can walk through. Now build a spike you cannot. That sounds like a small change — one checkbox — and it is going to break your game, because it will reveal something you have been carrying since 1.4: your character is a ghost. Today you fix that properly, and then build health, damage and death on top of the fix.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I take damage when I touch a spike?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Take damage when I touch a spike — "how do I take damage when I touch a spike?" — for a character that is currently a ghost: the physics engine knows it is standing there and has never once been asked to move it.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the spike a shape that pushes backA Collider2D on the Spikes prefab, sized to the art, with Is Trigger left off. That checkbox is where the spike stops being a coin: a trigger reports an overlap and pushes nothing, while a solid collider pushes — and a push is the only thing that can stop you. It has to sit on the object carrying the Spikes tag.Read: the OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D c) row in the quick reference, and the Is Trigger setting you used on the coin in 2.1.
  2. write this partRead: the rb.linearVelocity = v row and the Body Type warning in the quick reference, and the movement table earlier in this lesson.
  3. Confirm the thing you hit was a spikeOnCollisionEnter2D fires when solid colliders meet, and its parameter is a Collision2D — a container, not a collider — which is why the tag is asked of collision.gameObject rather than of collision itself. Same tag check as the coin, one level of indirection further out.Read: the OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D c) and other.CompareTag("Coin") rows in the quick reference.
  4. Take the damage, and stop at the floorHealth is a class-body field, and one method changes it by a signed amount so the same method can heal later. The subtraction is guarded: if health is already zero, return before touching the number, so it can never run to -1, -2, -3 and stop meaning anything.Read: the if (health <= 0) { ... } else { ... } row in the quick reference, and the coin count field you declared in 2.1.

Note which part is the gap and which three are last lesson's coin pickup wearing a different tag. You already know how to check a tag and how to change a value that lives in the class body. What is genuinely new is who moves the Player — and until that changes, a solid spike is a picture you can stand inside.

The test: does the part name the thing that does the work? "Take damage" is an effect, not a part. "Hand the movement to the physics engine" is a part — and it is the only one here that changes what your character is allowed to do.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Your coin count only ever goes up, so it needs no rule at all. Health only goes down, and it has a floor. Which part above keeps health inside the range where the number still means something — and what would the Console print on a second spike without it?

In 2.1 you wrote if (other.CompareTag("Coin")) and changed a number inside it. Which parts of today's split are that same shape, and which one is not?

1.4 and 1.5 built your movement twice — first with transform.Translate, then with a normalized direction. What did that movement never consult, and why is that the whole reason your spike did nothing?

2.1's coin was a trigger: it reported an overlap and pushed nothing. Today's spike is solid, so it pushes. Which part of the split is that difference in, and what does the push buy you that the report could not?

The Problem: Walk Into a Spike ~10 min

Step 1. The Overworld scene has no spikes placed at all. Drag two or three Assets/Prefabs/Spikes instances into the scene and put them somewhere you will walk.

Step 2. Open the Spikes prefab and give it a collider, the same way you gave the coin one in 2.1. Two differences: leave Is Trigger unchecked, because spikes are solid — and remember the collider has to sit on the object carrying the Spikes tag. Then drag its size until the green outline matches the art.

Step 3. Press Play and walk into your spike.

Tinker: The Ghost

  1. You gave the spike a solid collider. Walk into it. Did you stop, or pass straight through? Describe exactly what happened.
  2. Now walk into a wall. You gave the Player a Collider2D and a Rigidbody2D in 2.1 — so why does the wall still not stop you?
  3. Open the documentation for Transform.Translate. Find the sentence that says whether the physics engine is consulted, and quote it precisely.
  4. The spike, the wall and the coin all have colliders now. What single thing in the Player's movement code stands between your character and the physics world?
  5. Predict: if you keep transform.Translate and make the spike solid, what will your player be able to do to every wall in the game?
This is the most important bug in the unit — do not patch around it. Your character is a ghost that the physics engine knows about but is never asked to move. transform.Translate edits coordinates directly; it never consults physics, so it will happily place you inside a wall. Every collision feature from here to the end of the year — spikes, walls, doors, enemies, the boss — depends on the decision you are about to make in the next block. Make it deliberately, and be ready to defend it.
Read the Docs: Choose Your Movement Method ~20 min

You read this table in 1.5 as a prediction. Now it is a decision you have to live with for the rest of the year, so read the last two columns very carefully — and read the note underneath about the documentation being wrong, because someone has already fallen into it for you:

TechniqueHow it worksStops at walls?What it requires
transform.Translate(vector) Offsets coordinates directly. Never consults physics. No Nothing. This is what you have now.
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = vector States how fast the body is travelling; the physics engine performs the motion. Yes A Rigidbody2D with Body Type Dynamic. Movement is in units per second, so no Time.deltaTime.
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) Sweeps the body to a target position and tests the path as it goes. Yes — but only on a Dynamic body A Rigidbody2D with Body Type Dynamic. The docs recommend Kinematic, and that is the one body type where it does not work.
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) Applies a physical push; mass, drag and inertia all apply. Yes A Dynamic Rigidbody2D with a mass you will have to tune.
The documentation recommends the one combination that does not work. Read this carefully, because it is a lesson about reading documentation and not a trick. Unity's page for MovePosition ends with the note "MovePosition is intended for use with kinematic rigidbodies." But the same page also says that "if the rigidbody is kinematic then any collisions won't affect the rigidbody itself" — and the manual page on body types says a Kinematic body "only collides with Dynamic Rigidbody 2Ds and not the other Body Types."

Put together: on a Kinematic body, MovePosition moves you to wherever you asked and nothing stops you on the way. The recommended pairing is the broken one. The rule that survives contact with all of it is simpler: for anything in the world to stop you, your body must be Dynamic.

And that is why this course's answer is the row above it — linearVelocity, on a Dynamic body. It needs no fine print.
Why your coins still work either way. Triggers are the exception to every rule above: a collider with Is Trigger ticked reports the overlap to any body type, including Kinematic. So a coin picks up whether you are Dynamic or Kinematic, while a wall and a cave door only notice a Dynamic you. This is exactly why "it works in my game" is not the same as "it is right."

Choose, Then Justify

  1. Your character is a ghost. Which row fixes that with the smallest change to the code you have already written?
  2. This game is about exploring a world and being shot at by turrets. Do you want your movement to carry momentum? Which row gives you momentum whether you want it or not?
  3. Only one column in that table has the same value in every row that works. What is it, and why is that column the real decision rather than the technique you picked?
  4. Two of the four rows measure movement differently from the other one. Which two, and what does each of them not need that transform.Translate does?
  5. A cave entrance has a solid collider wired to a scene change. It has been dormant all year because your Player had no body. Now that you have one, would it fire if you made your body Kinematic? Say why, using the word collision and the word trigger differently.
  6. Your EnemyController, TurretController and Projectile are all still empty shells. Would an enemy or a bullet need a different row from the player? Argue a position.
  7. What evidence from your own build would make your justification convincing to another student — a measurement, a screenshot, a before-and-after?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“how do I stop my character walking through walls?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. The shape of your file stays exactly as it is — fields at class scope, input read in Update(). Only the lines that change what moves the character are left for you to write.

This build leaves 2 lines for you to write. Everything around them is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Keep a handle on the body

You gave the Player a Rigidbody2D in 2.1. To hand it instructions you need a reference to it, and you find that once — not sixty times a second.

    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;

    private Rigidbody2D body;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    void Start()
    {
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
    }
  1. 1Your existing speed knob. Unchanged.
  2. 3A field to hold the Player's Rigidbody2D component. Class body, not inside a method — the same rule from 1.3: this has to still be here on the next frame.
  3. 5Your existing input fields. Still declared here, still assigned in Update(). Nothing about 1.4 changes.
  4. 8The once-only setup method from 1.3. It has been empty until now — this is what it is for.
  5. 10Look up the Rigidbody2D sitting on this same GameObject and store it in body. GetComponent<T>() finds a component on the object the script is attached to.Once, in Start() — never in Update(). GetComponent is a search, and calling it every frame is 60 searches a second for an answer that never changes. Assigning it in Start() is the same "decide once, remember it" instinct as declaring inputX at class scope.

Step 2Compute the movement you already know how to compute

None of this is new — it is the vector from 1.4, rebuilt so it points somewhere rather than describing a distance.

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);

        body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed;
  1. 1Still the every-frame method. Start() ran once; Update() runs from now until you stop playing.
  2. 3Assign, not declare. Same two lines, same reasoning, as 1.4.
  3. 6The two axis values, packed into one vector. This is a direction now, not a distance — it says which way, not how far.
  4. Your turn8Hand the body a velocity instead of moving the Transform yourself. This one line replaces transform.Translate(movement);, and it is the whole fix.You want the property on body that says how fast it is travelling, set to direction multiplied by moveSpeed. In Unity 6 that property is no longer called velocity.Two things changed at once, and both matter. First, you are asking the physics engine to do the moving — so it knows where you are going and can stop you. Second, there is no Time.deltaTime. Velocity is already measured *per second*, so the engine applies the time for you. Multiplying by deltaTime here is the most common mistake on this line.

Step 3Finish the step and prove it

Close the method, then make the settings in the Inspector match what you just wrote.

//   Body Type          =  Dynamic
//   Gravity Scale      =  0
//   Freeze Rotation Z  ☑ ON
//   Interpolate        =  Interpolate
  1. 1Closes Update(). One more } closes the class.
  2. 4Must be Dynamic. This is the setting the whole lesson turns on — only a Dynamic body is stopped by the world. Still what you set in 2.1: leave it.If you are tempted to switch this to Kinematic because the MovePosition documentation tells you to, read the next activity before you do. A Kinematic body "only collides with Dynamic Rigidbody 2Ds and not the other Body Types" — so it walks straight through your walls and through your cave doors.
  3. 5Already 0 from 2.1. Top-down worlds have no down.
  4. Your turn6Stop the body from spinning: find the Constraints section of the Rigidbody 2D and freeze rotation on the Z axis. This is an Inspector setting, so record it as a comment in your file.In 2.1 you left Constraints alone, because nothing in the world was solid to you.This did not matter in 2.1 — a trigger reports an overlap without pushing anything, so nothing could ever spin you. A solid collider does push, and an off-centre hit imparts torque. Without this, your character tumbles like a dropped coin the first time it hits a wall at an angle.
  5. 7Already set in 2.1. Keeps movement smooth between physics steps.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • Body Type set to Kinematic, because the MovePosition docs said so

    You will seeThe character walks through every wall and every cave door exactly as before, and nothing in the Console complains.

    Do thisBody Type = Dynamic. A Kinematic body only collides with Dynamic bodies — static walls and cave entrances are invisible to it. Triggers are the one exception, which is why your coins still work and makes the whole thing more confusing.

  • body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;

    You will seeThe character moves, but at a crawl — roughly one sixtieth of the speed you asked for.

    Do thisDrop Time.deltaTime. Velocity is measured in units per second, so the physics engine already multiplies by time. deltaTime belongs with transform.Translate, which moves a distance per frame. Different unit, different formula.

  • transform.Translate(...) left in place alongside the new velocity line

    You will seeThe character moves at roughly double speed, and still slides through walls — because Translate is still doing the moving.

    Do thisThe two lines fight each other. Delete the transform.Translate line and the Vector2 movement that fed it. One object, one thing moving it.

  • GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>() called inside Update() instead of assigned in Start()

    You will seeNothing visibly breaks, so the mistake survives review — a component search repeated 60 times a second, forever.

    Do thisAssign body once in Start(). If you also forgot the assignment entirely, body stays null and the first frame throws a NullReferenceException.

  • the Player's collider left on the Untagged Sprite child

    You will seeCoins work, but the cave entrance never opens — even though you are now Dynamic.

    Do thisThe collider must be on the root, the object tagged Player. SceneSwitch asks collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player"), and collision.gameObject is whichever object owns the collider.

  • the spike made solid while its collider is not fitted to the sprite art

    You will seeYou take damage from standing well clear of the spikes, or you walk visually through the tips without harm.

    Do thisSelect the collider and drag its size until the green outline in the Scene view matches the art. A new collider does not fit itself to your sprite.

  • subtracting health inside OnCollisionEnter2D but never checking whether the player is already dead

    You will seeHealth runs to −3, −4, −5 on repeated contacts. The number stops meaning anything.

    Do thisGuard the subtraction with the death condition, so the value stays inside the range that is meaningful — the same "a value needs a rule, not just arithmetic" idea you meet properly in 2.3.

Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The two gaps are body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed; and the frozen Z rotation, and neither of them is right by luck: the first has no deltaTime because velocity is per second, the second exists because solid collisions push.

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;
    [SerializeField] private int health = 3;
    [SerializeField] private int coins;

    private Rigidbody2D body;

    private float inputX;
    private float inputY;

    void Start()
    {
        // Look the component up ONCE. Never inside Update().
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        inputX = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        inputY = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(inputX, inputY);

        // No Time.deltaTime: velocity is per second, not per frame.
        body.linearVelocity = direction * moveSpeed;
    }

    private void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision)
    {
        // Collision2D, not Collider2D — so the tag is asked of .gameObject.
        if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Spikes"))
        {
            TakeDamage(1);
        }
    }

    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            coins = coins + 1;
            Debug.Log("Coins collected: " + coins);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }

    private void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        if (health <= 0)
        {
            return;
        }

        health = health - amount;
        Debug.Log("Health: " + health);

        if (health <= 0)
        {
            Debug.Log("Player died.");
        }
    }
}

// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ Rigidbody 2D:
//   Body Type          =  Dynamic     <- only Dynamic is stopped by the world
//   Gravity Scale      =  0           <- top-down world, no down
//   Freeze Rotation Z  =  ON          <- solid hits impart spin
//   Interpolate        =  Interpolate

Read the Docs: How Should a Spike Hurt You? ~15 min

A spike is solid, so it stops you. But "stopping you" and "hurting you" are two separate decisions. Here are the three honest ways to build a hazard:

ApproachWhat the player feelsWhat firesThe risk
Solid spike + OnCollisionEnter2D You stop against it. Damage once per touch. OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) You can get wedged against the spike, and sliding along it may not register at all.
Trigger spike + OnTriggerEnter2D You walk through it. Damage once per entry. OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) Standing inside the spike deals no further damage — usually wrong for a hazard.
Trigger spike + OnTriggerStay2D with a cooldown Repeated damage while you stand in it. OnTriggerStay2D(Collider2D other) It fires every frame. Without a cooldown you lose all your health instantly.
The parameter types are different, and it matters. OnTrigger* hands you a Collider2D, which has .gameObject and .CompareTag directly. OnCollision* hands you a Collision2D, which is a data container carrying contact points, relativeVelocity, and .gameObject. That is why one lets you write other.CompareTag(...) and the other makes you write collision.gameObject.CompareTag(...).

Picking a Hazard Model

  1. Which of the three matches the game you are building? Which would you pick for a game where spikes are a puzzle to be solved rather than a hazard to be avoided?
  2. In the third row, what happens on the very first frame the player stands in the spike if you forget the cooldown? How many times per second does OnTriggerStay2D run?
  3. For which of the three can you write other.CompareTag("Spikes") directly, and what must you write for the others?
  4. Should a spike be destroyed when it damages you, the way a coin is destroyed when collected? What kind of object is a spike, and what does that tell you about using Destroy here?

Architectural specification: health.
  • Following the decision you made in 2.1, where does health live, and what field holds it? What type, what starting value, and how is it exposed as a tuning knob?

Death has more than one defensible design. Choose one, and defend it.
  • (a) Reload the current scene — SceneManager.LoadScene(SceneManager.GetActiveScene().buildIndex). Everything resets, including the coin count.
  • (b) Reload a scene by name — before you pick this, read Build Settings and answer two questions: which scene is index 0, and does that scene contain a Player?
  • (c) Do not reload at all — reset health and move the player back to a starting position, keeping the coins.

The Death Decision

  1. Which death design did you choose, and what does the player keep and lose under it?
  2. Option (b) loads this project's scene 0. What is in that scene, and what would the player actually see after dying? Test it before you answer.

Bug Hunt ~15 min

Bug Hunt: Physics and Boundary Faults

  1. Set the spike's collider back to Is Trigger but keep your collision callback. Does anything fire? What does the Console show — or fail to show?
  2. Set Body Type to Kinematic and walk into a wall. You are now following the documentation's own advice — does it stop you? Then walk into a cave door: does the scene still change? Explain both results with one sentence about what a Kinematic body collides with.
  3. Put your velocity line back to multiplying by Time.deltaTime. Measure roughly how much slower the character moves, and compare that against the physics timestep.
  4. Delete the if (health <= 0) check and stand in a spike. What does the health number do? What does that prove about the difference between a rule and a value?
  5. If you used the OnTriggerStay2D model, remove the cooldown and describe the first half-second of contact.
  6. Set your speed very high and run at a wall. Do you stop, or end up on the other side? What does the wall's thickness have to do with it? (This failure has a name — look up "tunnelling".)
  7. Die on purpose and watch the Console. Which values reset, and which survived? Compare that against what you wrote down earlier — were you right?
